opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's been a lot harder than I imagined, but also more meaningful than I expected.

When you're in academia, or even at a big industrial lab, your job is mostly to think clearly about research problems. You pick a direction, you work with students or collaborators, you write papers, and the feedback loop, while slow, is relatively well defined. Building a company is completely different. Suddenly you're responsible for people's careers, for hiring, for fundraising, for making decisions with very incomplete information, and you can't just say "let's run another ablation" before committing.

There were definitely moments early on where I asked myself, did I make the right choice? Because research is something I love, and I was quite comfortable there. But what pushed me was the feeling that some of the questions I care about most, especially around how AI systems can really understand the visual and physical world rather than just language, need a different kind of organization to pursue. You need compute, you need engineering at scale, you need a team that's aligned on one long-term bet. It's hard to do that purely inside a university.

So my feeling now is that I don't regret it. It's exhausting, and I'm learning things every week that I never had to think about as a researcher. But it also forces you to be honest: does this idea actually work, does it matter to anyone outside a paper? I think that pressure is healthy. And I still see myself as a researcher at heart. The company is, in a way, just a bigger and more demanding version of a lab, where the experiment is whether this vision can really become real.

r001.rationale: The response describes the work as hard and meaningful, but does not say that internal friction gradually eases as the company grows or that watching this happen is enjoyable.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's a question I ask myself almost every week. For most of my career I was a researcher, first at FAIR and then at NYU, and the rhythm of that life is very different. You pick a problem, you go deep, you write a paper, and the feedback loop is measured in months. Building a company compresses everything. The feedback loop is daily, sometimes hourly, and the problems are not just technical anymore. You're thinking about people, about hiring, about what to say no to, about money.

I think the honest answer is that I don't regret it, but I underestimated how much of it is not the part I'm good at. I thought the hardest thing would be the research, because that's what I'd always optimized for. It turns out the research is the part I find restful. The hard part is prioritization under uncertainty. In academia you can afford to be curious about everything. In a company, curiosity is a cost, and you have to decide which three things actually matter this quarter and let the rest go. That's painful for someone who got into this field because they liked chasing interesting questions.

What pushed me over the edge was a feeling I had around the time of some of our later work on visual representations and generative models. I kept seeing ideas that I believed were right, and I kept watching them not make it into the world because the gap between a paper and something people actually use was just too wide for a lab to close. You can write the paper, you can release the code, and then it sits there. I wanted to see whether the ideas I believed in would survive contact with real users. That's a different kind of validation than citations, and I think I was hungry for it.

The other thing I'd say is that it changed how I think about research itself. When you have to ship, you quickly learn which parts of your taste were real and which were just academic fashion. Some things I used to care about a lot, I now think were about looking clever at conferences. And some things I used to dismiss as engineering turned out to be where all the actual leverage is. Data, evaluation, infrastructure. Those are not glamorous, but they decide whether something works.

So would I do it again? Yes, but I'd tell my earlier self to be less romantic about it. Being an entrepreneur isn't a bigger version of being a researcher. It's a different job that happens to use some of the same skills. The part that surprised me most is that I enjoy it even on the days when I'm clearly bad at it. That's probably the best sign I had that it was the right call.

r001.rationale: The candidate says entrepreneurship is enjoyable even on difficult days, but does not describe enjoying internal friction gradually easing as the company grows.

astra-6.text:
I think I’m still discovering what that decision means. Before starting a company, you can imagine the research you want to do and the product you want to build. Once you’re actually doing it, the question becomes much more concrete: What should we work on today? Who do we need on the team? How do we know we’re building something useful?

That’s been a big adjustment, but I enjoy the connection between those decisions. Your research choices affect the product, and what you learn from building the product changes the research questions. There’s a lot of uncertainty, and some days are frustrating. But so far, the experience has made me more excited about the decision. I want to see what we can build.

r001.rationale: The response says the speaker enjoys how research and product decisions inform each other, but does not describe internal friction easing as the company grows.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s still too early to say whether it was the right decision, but I’m enjoying the process. As a researcher, you can focus very deeply on one problem. When you’re building a company, you have to think about the team, the product, and whether what you’re doing actually matters to users. You can’t just say, “That’s outside my area.” You have to take responsibility for the whole thing.

That’s challenging, but it’s also what makes it exciting. For me, the motivation is still to build something I really believe in. Starting a company is a way to pursue that, rather than an end in itself.

r001.rationale: The candidate says building a company is challenging and exciting, but does not mention internal friction easing as the company grows.
